The bill would increase the money available for research programs run by the Australian Research Council by adding an extra $829.052 million over four years.

It would raise the maximum funding caps in the Australian Research Council Act 2001 by applying standard inflation adjustments to three existing annual figures and adding a new figure for the year starting 1 July 2022.
The changes affect only the special appropriation mechanism and do not change the substance of the Act, and the bill does not engage any human rights.
Apply indexation rates to existing appropriation amounts for the financial years starting 1 July 2019, 1 July 2020 and 1 July 2021.
Add a new appropriation for the financial year starting 1 July 2022, extending the forward estimate period.
Increase the total special appropriation by $829.052 million for the period 1 July 2019 to 30 June 2023.
The Australian Research Council and the research programs it administers under the National Competitive Grants Program.
Australian Research Council Amendment Bill 2019 - Second Reading - Research cuts
Australian Research Council Amendment Bill 2019 - Consideration in Detail - Anouncement process

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2020-02-11.13.1) introduced by NSW Senator [Mehreen Faruqi](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/nsw/mehreen_faruqi) (Greens), which means it failed. The amendment is an attempt to address the politicisation of the grants process. ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 1, page 3 (after line 11), at the end of the Schedule, add:* > > *4 After section 51* > > *Insert:* > > *51A Announcements about approval of expenditure on research programs* > > *(1) The Minister must, within 21 days after making a determination under paragraph 51(2) (b):* > >>*(a) make a public announcement of the determination; and* >> >> *(b) cause a copy of the announcement to be published on the internet.* > > *(2) The Minister must not make an announcement under subsection (1) together with any of the following:* > >> *(a) another member of parliament;* >> >> *(b) a candidate in an election for the Senate or the House of Representatives.* > > *(3) An announcement made under subsection (1) is not a legislative instrument.* > > *(4) To avoid doubt, subsection (1) applies in addition to subsection 51(3).* > > *(5) In this section, member of parliament means:* > >> *(a) a senator; or* >> >> *(b) a member of the House of Representatives; or* >> >> *(c) a Minister of State who is not a senator or member of the House of Representatives; or* >> >> *(d) a person who is taken to be the President of the Senate under the Parliamentary Presiding Officers Act 1965 and who is not a senator or member of the House of Representatives; or* >> >> *(e) a person who is taken to be the Speaker of the House of Representatives under the Parliamentary Presiding Officers Act 1965 and who is not a senator or member of the House of Representatives.*

The Australian Research Council Amendment Bill 2019 was introduced to update funding caps in the ARC Act until 30 June 2023, enabling continued ARC grant funding. The bill supports over $3 billion in ARC research funding over four years, with cited examples including a $5 million lobster aquaculture hub and a $1 million Indigenous cultural learning project.

Labor will not oppose the Australian Research Council Amendment Bill 2019 but criticised the government for cutting $328.5 million from research funding over four years, interfering in independent peer-reviewed grants, and failing to invest in education and research infrastructure.

The coalition government has cut federal R&D expenditure by 19% in real terms between 2015-16 and 2017-18, and Australia's R&D spending as a share of GDP is 1.8% against the OECD average of 2.4%; only 7% of mid-career NHMRC grant applications were funded, and 61% of young scientists have considered leaving the country to continue their research.

The speaker supported the ARC Amendment Bill but criticised the government for cutting research funding, interfering in peer-reviewed grants (including 11 grants totalling $4.2 million secretly vetoed by the minister, mostly in humanities and social sciences), and abandoning the Education Investment Fund.

Centre Alliance supported the bill but criticised the politicisation of ARC grants, citing the 2018 blocking of 11 humanities grants and a new staggered announcement process that delays recruitment and harms Australia's research competitiveness.

The bill amends funding gaps in the ARC Act to support research, with announcements of $24 million for training centres, $242 million for centres of excellence, and $54 million for Laureate Fellows, including Professors Belinda Medlyn and Lynette Russell. The ARC’s Gender and the research workforce report showed a slight improvement in the male-to-female researcher ratio from 57:43 in 2015 to 56:44 in 2018.
